name: Bena
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
catalog_citation: Morrison, Michelle Elizabeth. 2011. A Reference Grammar of Bena. PhD dissertation, Rice University, Houston (chair Claire Bowern), xxx+515 pp. hdl:1911/70359 (Rice DSpace open item).
catalog_quote: [p.52 fn.9] Though the penultimate and antepenultimate syllables of a word are common locations for stress cross-linguistically, Bena does not have a stress system. In a stress system, each word would must contain a stressed syllable. This means that if length were a manifestation of stress in Bena each word would have to contain a long vowel. However, in Bena it is possible to have a word that has only short syllables (for example libihi 'tree'). [p.64] Morae may be either High toned or toneless, and each word is assigned a single High tone. With only a few exceptions, word-final tone is disallowed. Odden (1988) has argued that Bena tone falls within what he refers to as "predictable tone systems." In such systems, the location of High is largely predictable on the basis of phonological shape and/or verbal tense and aspect. [p.69] A word allows at maximum a single High tone. [p.70] Major tonal patterns in Bena (described in terms of the position where the High tone falls) include penultimate (PU), antepenultimate (APU), stem-initial (SI), and pre-stem initial (PSI). There are a few very specific situations in which word-final (WF) tone is allowed. ... Location of High tone is consistent, regardless of frame. This means that a word pronounced in isolation has the same tone pattern as one that occurs in a sentence. [p.92] Swahili has a stress-based system; Bena's system is tonal (though it does have a reduced tonal system when compared with many other Bantu languages).
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Bena (bena1262, Bantu G63) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Philippson 1991 (theses.fr 1992PA05H011), was already held by the project (mwal1237/) and is now copied under bena1262/ and read: §2.6.1 pp. 442-444 and the synthesis card p. 508 treat Bena as an accentual language with an H* melody — two 'accent' patterns, penultimate (PB *BB/*BH stems) vs. prefix (*HB/*HH), analysed metrically with an extrametrical final syllable; he does not claim stress. The best first-hand statement is Morrison 2011 (Rice PhD, held by the project, text verified): fn. 9 p. 52 'Bena does not have a stress system', §2.3 p. 64 'each word is assigned a single High tone', §2.3.5 p. 92 'Bena's system is tonal'. Crossref abstract of Morrison 2014 and archive.org snippets of Odden 1988 agree (one predictable H per word). Not obtainable by automated download: Schumann 1917/18 ZfK 8 (not digitised on archive.org; HathiTrust/BSB/SUB-HH blocked), Eaton 2007 SIL sketch and Mitterhofer 2013 (sil.org an automated-access block), Persée PDF (altcha); Semantic Scholar, Google Books and web search quotas were exhausted. Recommended coding if added: no word stress; culminative predictable tone (pitch accent type).

new_statements.rule_in_words: The author states explicitly that Bena has no stress system; prominence is tonal: a restricted ('predictable') tone system with at most one High per word, whose position (penultimate mora, antepenultimate mora, stem-initial, or pre-stem-initial) is determined lexically for nouns and by tense-aspect for verbs. Phonemic and derived vowel length is confined to the penult/antepenult but is argued not to be stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final High allowed only in a few cases (possessive clitic); dialectal variation in which tone pattern (PSI/APU/PU) nouns and verb forms take; younger speakers show reduced High/Low pitch range under Swahili influence, described as possible incipient shift toward a stress-based system.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; Morrison states the location of High is the same in isolation and in sentence context (p.70: 'a word pronounced in isolation has the same tone pattern as one that occurs in a sentence'). Analysis based mainly on the Ngaveta dialect (Njombe district, fieldwork 2008-2009).
new_statements.identity_note: Morrison's analysis is based mainly on the Ngaveta dialect of Bena (Njombe district); she reports dialectal variation in tone-pattern distribution across Nyikolwe, Mavemba, Twangabita, Sovi, Maswamu, Ngaveta but the no-stress/tonal characterization is given for Bena as a whole (bena1262). Not to be confused with Bena of Nigeria (Adamawa).

new_statements.reading: Bena has no word stress. Its word prosody is a restricted ('predictable') tone system: at most one High (phonetically high-falling) tone per word, positioned by rule on the penultimate, antepenultimate, pre-stem-initial or stem-initial mora depending on stem shape and tense/aspect; word-final H is nearly disallowed. Philippson 1991 (pp. 442-444, 508), read in the same search, gives the same picture in accentual terms ('langue accentuelle à mélodie H*': penultimate accent for etymologically low stems, prefix accent for etymologically high stems). If Bena is added to the catalog it should be coded as a culminative-tone / pitch accent language with no stress, not as a penultimate-stress language.

new_statements.quote: Bena has two tones: High (H) and Low (L), though Low tone is more accurately described as toneless. Phonological words can only have a single H, which is assigned at the level of the mora. [...] In general, word‑final H is disallowed, though there are a few situations where morphophonological processes can result in word‑final H. Verbal roots in Bena are underlyingly toneless (/gon‑a/ 'sleep'), as are subject and object markers. Surface forms may have at most a single High‑toned mora. Inflected forms display several different tone patterns. There are four tone melodies; choice of melody is predictable primarily on the basis of morphological criteria.

new_statements.relation_note: On word stress as such the article is silent. On word prosody it agrees with, and adds detail to, the Morrison 2011 statements already held by the project (no stress system; one predictable H per word on PU / APU / stem-initial / pre-stem-initial mora): it spells out the four melodies and their morphological conditioning, and states that the analysis is of the Ngaveta dialect. The catalog record for Bena has an empty rule field; nothing here supports a stress placement, and a catalog entry should stay 'no word stress; one culminative predictable H tone per word'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The article is about tone only: the words stress, accent and prominence never occur in the body (only in the title of the Odden 1988 reference). Bena is described as a restricted tone language with at most one High tone per phonological word, assigned to a mora; verb roots, subject and object markers are toneless; the H of an inflected verb is placed by one of four melodies named after the mora that carries it -- pre-stem-initial (PSI: remote future -la-, hortative -ha-, negative infinitive -ta-), macrostem-initial (MSI: perfect -ile forms and anteriors), antepenultimate (APU: -a forms with monomorphemic bases, e.g. infinitive, present, near future) and penultimate (PU: -a forms with polymorphemic bases, imperfective/narrative -ag, subjunctives, imperatives, itives) -- with the choice predictable from morphology (prefix, final suffix, base complexity, negation). Word-final H is generally disallowed; a rising LH on a long vowel is repaired by Leftward Shift (H moves one mora left). Nouns (p. 325): toneless stems put H on the class prefix; stems with underlying H have it on the antepenultimate or penultimate mora; -i/-o nominalizations take APU from underived and PU from derived verbs, -e nominalizations take PSI. No statement about stress, positive or negative.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (no stress discussed at all); only one H per word, so no secondary tonal peak.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final H arises in some subjunctives (ndifwé 'that I die') and in PU forms with imbrication; CV monosyllabic stems put the MSI H on the pre-stem mora instead (ndífwe 'I died'); a few -i/-o nominalizations of underived verbs have PU instead of the expected APU (hilímo 'agriculture', himélo 'plant', lunyílo 'speed'), p. 325-326.
new_statements.identity_note: Morrison 2014 describes the Ngaveta dialect of Bena, spoken in the north-west of the Bena area (Njombe District, Tanzania), data 2007-2009; it notes significant dialectal variation in the tone system and that Eaton 2007 describes a different dialect (LH/HL contrast on long vowels).

tone_statements.quote: Bena is a restricted tone language in which only one high tone is allowed per word. In this respect, Bena resembles the closely related language Kinga (G65). In a study on tone in Kinga, Schadeberg (1973), notes that a high tone may occur in one of three possible positions: on the antepenultimate (APU) mora, on the pre-stem-initial (PSI) mora or on the penultimate (PU) mora. Thus no word ends in a high tone. These three tone patterns are also found in Bena nouns, however Bena verbs also attest a stem-initial (SI) tone pattern. In this description, short vowels are analysed as having one mora and phonemically long vowels and compensatory lengthened vowels are analysed as having two morae.

sources.quote: Verbal tone in Bena is characterized by a single High tone per word. Roots are toneless, and inflected forms are assigned one of four tone melodies : Pre‑Stem Initial (PSI), Macrostem Initial (MSI), Antepenultimate (APU), and Penultimate (PU). The location of H in an inflected form is entirely predictable through a combination of morphophonological criteria, including the morphological complexity of the verbal base, the tense and aspect of the verb, the form of the final suffix, and whether the verb is affirmative or negative.
sources.note: Peer-reviewed published version of the dissertation's tone chapter; may restate or refine the no-stress / culminative-H analysis and would be the citable journal source.
